newsitem.title: UK: Nationalists walk down "their" Garvaghy Road.
newsitem.headline: Nationalists walk down "their" Garvaghy Road.

text.p: Thousands of Catholics marched down Portadown's Garvaghy Road on Wednesday night in a peaceful protest at the way Britain allowed the Orange Order to parade the same half-mile (one km) on Sunday.

A discreet police and army presence kept watch from a distance in sharp contrast to the massive security operation that was assembled before dawn on Sunday to protect the Orange Order in its disputed march past Catholic homes.

They carried placards saying "No Justice, No Peace" and "Reroute Sectarian Marches" in a protest against plans to hold two more Protestant parades in Catholic areas on Saturday, climax of the Protestant "marching season."

Gerry Adams, president of the Irish Republican Army's (IRA) political wing, Sinn Fein, marched with a crowd estimated at up to 5,000 Irish nationalists who see Dublin as the capital of a reunited Ireland.

But Adams ceded the speakers' platform to leaders of Catholic residents associations who are demanding that the Orange Order reroute parades down Belfast's Lower Ormeau Road and Londonderry on Saturday.

Gerard Rice, the Ormeau Road residents association spokesman, appealed to "right-thinking Catholics across Ireland to stop work for two hours on Friday" in an island-wide protest at Britain's handling of contentious parades.

He vilified British Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, who authorised one of the biggest security operations in the province's history to guard 1,200 Orange faithful down the road that bisects a Catholic housing estate in this southern town.
Mowlam said on Tuesday that Rice's organisation had broken off contact with her on talks to find a compromise over the Ormeau Road march.

She made the assertion after a leaked government document was interpreted as showing that the decision to allow the parade was taken weeks before it was announced and despite last-minute negotiations to find a compromise over the route.

One section of the document said her advisers had decided to allow "Orange feet on the Garvaghy Road." The decision sparked the worst Catholic violence the province has seen since civil rights marches in the 1970s.
Rice denied he had broken off talks but suggested that a decision to allow the Ormeau Road march had already been taken and invitations to negotiations were a sham.
"We will talk to her, but we want to see her gameplan first," he said. "And it's Orange feet on the Lower Ormeau Road," he said to jeers from the crowd.
"There will be no Orange feet on the Ormeau Road," he added, to loud applause.

He appealed to "everyone present" to make their way to Belfast on Saturday to prevent the parade. A similar appeal has been issued by Londonderry catholics who want to prevent an Orange Parade through the Catholic town on Saturday.
